title: Clausewitz und Moltke haben unser Führungsproblem gelöst. Wir haben es nur nicht gelernt.
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Written in German, this essay by product-development leader Uwe Mierisch separates leadership from management using John Kotter's distinction (management copes with complexity, leadership copes with change) and the Prussian military thinkers Clausewitz and Moltke. He argues that organisations work on three levels rather than two: a stable purpose set by the executive team as trustees of the owners, strategy as the continual re-assessment of the situation after every move, and tactics carried out by teams who decide as close to events as possible. Moltke's mission command means saying what is to be achieved and why while leaving the how to the person on the spot. Drawing on Drucker, he holds that leadership is an activity, not a position, and that a boss is someone who takes responsibility for what others do, which requires making a real contribution rather than just holding the line. Management is described as the deployment that reduces execution complexity, and he contrasts it with tracking and monitoring, which only record what was not done. The piece belongs to his NewPDP series on development models.
points: Leadership and management are different jobs, and most companies are well administered but poorly led because calendars favour reports and budgets.
Purpose, strategy and tactics are three distinct levels of work, each led by setting direction and aligning people, with purpose kept stable over many years.
Moltke's mission command works only when people know the why and operate inside a system with shared rhythm, visible tasks and clear responsibilities.
A boss is defined by taking responsibility for the actions of others, and that responsibility is a gamble unless the boss contributes and stays close to the work.
Real management creates preconditions for execution, whereas tracking, surveillance and justification merely report what was not accomplished.
quotes: Ein gutes Fahrzeug baut niemand allein. Es entsteht aus Tausenden von Entscheidungen, die Hunderte von Menschen treffen.
Management bewältigt Komplexität. Es plant, budgetiert, organisiert und kontrolliert. Es sorgt dafür, dass ein großes System verlässlich läuft.
Führung bewältigt Veränderung. Sie setzt eine Richtung, richtet die Menschen darauf aus und bringt sie in Bewegung.
Strategie ist das, was zwischen Zweck und Plan passiert: nach jedem Zug neu bewerten, wo man steht, und den nächsten Zug wählen.
Der Vorgesetzte sagt, was erreicht werden soll und warum. Das Wie entscheidet der, der vor Ort ist.
Verantwortung ohne eigenen Beitrag ist keine Verantwortung. Sie ist ein Glücksspiel.
Management schafft Voraussetzungen. Tracking stellt fest, was nicht erledigt wurde.
